```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5
)
library(cusumtests)
```

## Fit an ordered regression

Recursive residuals are standardized one-step-ahead prediction errors.
Their order determines the paths, so arrange the data in the order you want
to test before fitting the regression. The first `k` rows of the fitted design
must identify all `k` coefficients, and at least two fitted rows must follow.

The monthly `Seatbelts` data are already in chronological order. The
following example models the number of drivers killed as a function of
distance driven and petrol price.

```{r fit}
belts <- as.data.frame(datasets::Seatbelts)
month <- seq(as.Date("1969-01-01"), by = "month", length.out = nrow(belts))
fit <- lm(DriversKilled ~ log(kms) + PetrolPrice, data = belts)
```

## Run CUSUM and CUSUMQ

`cusum()` adds the signed recursive residuals. Persistent forecast errors
of the same sign can pull its path away from zero. `cusumq()` adds the squared
residuals as shares of their total. Its path can depart from the diagonal
when large forecast errors are concentrated in part of the sample.
`cusumQ()` is an alias for `cusumq()`.

Pass a `time` vector to label the horizontal axis. It needs one entry per
fitted row after any subsetting or omission of missing values. Both tests use
all three significance levels by default.

```{r both-tests}
signed <- cusum(fit, B = 4999, seed = 17, time = month)
squared <- cusumq(fit, B = 4999, seed = 17, time = month)

signed
squared$decisions
```

The printed p-value describes the largest departure over the path. The
decision table gives the cutoff and rejection indicator at each level. A
failure to reject means the observed departure was compatible with the
reference at that level.

## Plot and inspect the bands

The default plot displays the path and every calculated band. Pass `alpha`
to display a subset of the stored levels using the existing calibration.

```{r plots, fig.show="hold"}
plot(signed, xlab = "Month")
plot(squared, alpha = 0.05, xlab = "Month")
```

The `data` component has one row per recursive residual and significance
level. Inspect one level to get a single copy of the path and its bounds.

```{r band-data}
band_5 <- subset(squared$data, alpha == 0.05)
head(band_5)

crossed <- with(band_5, cusumq < lower | cusumq > upper)
any(crossed)
squared$p.value <= 0.05
```

For a result containing only 5% bands and decisions, pass `alpha` to the test.

```{r one-level}
cusum(fit, alpha = 0.05, B = 4999, seed = 17)$decisions
```

## Detect a simulated mean shift

Here the observations are independent, with the second half shifted by
1.5 units. The fitted intercept assumes a constant mean throughout.

```{r mean-shift}
set.seed(42)
observation <- seq_len(160)
response <- rnorm(length(observation)) + 1.5 * (observation > 80)
shift_fit <- lm(response ~ 1)

shift_test <- cusum(shift_fit, B = 4999, seed = 17)
shift_test
plot(shift_test, alpha = 0.05)
```

A crossing gives evidence against the reference model. The time of that
crossing can differ from the date the underlying change first occurred.

## Choose the calibration settings

For each test, the same null draws determine the Monte Carlo p-value and
the critical values for the simultaneous bands. Use `seed` to reproduce
the calibration with the same random-number settings. When a result is
near a threshold, a larger `B` reduces simulation variability.

The finite-sample reference assumes fixed regressors and independent,
homoskedastic Gaussian errors under the null. Residual dependence,
heteroskedasticity, heavy tails, and lagged outcomes can change the
reference distribution. The `Seatbelts` regression illustrates the
workflow with monthly data, where serial dependence and seasonality are
plausible. See `help("cusum", package = "cusumtests")` for model
requirements and the full result structure.
